payload.headline: Alphabet slips to 280.2, below 282.31; falling forecasts keep me waiting for 277.07

summary.thesis: Sales are growing fast and margins are improving, but heavy spending has cut free cash flow from 73.6B to 19.7B and profit forecasts keep falling, so the price of 280.2 sits at the top of fair value rather than below it.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait, and buy at the 277.07 support level. Swing: no trade until a daily close holds inside 271.77–277.07.

payload.happening: Alphabet fell 1.24% to 280.2. That is just below 282.31, the middle of its own-history value range, and just above the 271.77–277.07 support zone. California reportedly banned Waymo from all state freeways, and Waymo reportedly paused freeway rides nationwide. It was also reported that former DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis's AI company raised $5 billion. No earnings date is in the data.
payload.business: The core business is still strong. Quarterly revenue grew 24.65% from a year earlier, up from 21.79% two quarters ago. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 33.32% from 32.19%. The balance sheet is safe: net cash is 139.0B and liquidity is 265.1B. Cash is what changed. Free cash flow, the cash left after all spending, fell to 19.7B from 73.6B, a free-cash-flow margin of only 4.19%. Each dollar invested now earns 24¢ a year, down from 40¢ three years ago, so the heavy spending is not paying back yet. Reported profit also looks better than it is: net margin of 50.03% is above the 33.32% operating margin because of one-off gains, so underlying earnings are lower. Today's news mostly affects sentiment and governance, not the core business. The Waymo freeway order hits a side project whose numbers are not in our data. Keeping Gemini chats for 2 months instead of 72 hours is a privacy and governance question. The Hassabis funding story is a talent and competition signal (general knowledge). The Gemini Tasks rollout is a product step, and no revenue numbers come with it. At risk: earnings quality and the payback on spending. Not at risk: demand, solvency or cash on hand.

worth.text: The methods disagree sharply. A discounted cash flow model (DCF), which values the company on its future cash, gives 25.89 to 69.81 with a base of 51.18. That is far below the price because the model starts from trailing free cash flow of 19.7B. Even 30% starting growth only lifts it to 77.21. So the gap comes from the cash starting point, not the growth rate. Against its own history, the stock is priced at 7.4 times sales, its 54th percentile over 5 years. That puts the price of 280.2 next to the own-history middle of 282.31, inside a 234.35–375.22 range. Against peers it looks expensive: the peer median is 5.0 times sales, and the growth-adjusted ratio is 1.31. On earnings, it trades at 14.7 times trailing profit but 18.7 times next year's, because analysts expect earnings per share to drop from 19.56 to 14.97. Filings note that the price needs about 38% a year growth, compared with 17% a year delivered over 3 years. My range runs from the own-history low to the own-history middle. The DCF result tells me not to pay above that middle.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow recovers from 19.7B toward the earlier 73.6B once the current spending cycle pays off; if it stays near 19.7B, even 234.35 is generous.

bull: Revenue growth is speeding up: 24.65% year on year last quarter, versus 21.79% two quarters ago.
Operating margin rose to 33.32% from 32.19%, so growth is not coming at the cost of profitability.
Net cash of 139.0B and a price-to-sales ratio at only the 54th percentile of its own 5-year history give a cushion.
bear: Free cash flow fell to 19.7B from 73.6B, which puts the cash-flow value at 51.18 per share.
Analysts cut this year's earnings-per-share estimate by 5.2% in 30 days, and they expect next year's to drop to 14.97 from 19.56.
At 7.4 times sales against a peer median of 5.0, the price needs about 38% a year growth, compared with 17% delivered.

levels.what: Top of the 271.77–277.07 support zone, tested 3 times. The first buy level, below the 282.31 own-history middle.
Bottom of the support zone. A daily close below it cancels the 277.07 buy and moves the next buy down to 234.35.
Low end of the own-history range. The add level, because it leaves room for error if free cash flow stays near 19.7B.

longterm.why: The price has slipped just under 282.31, but earnings forecasts are still falling and cash flow has not recovered. Buying at the 277.07 support level improves the trade-off.

swing.why: The 20-day and 50-day averages are both falling (297.39 and 325.93), and the trend is a range. The 271.77–277.07 support zone is narrower than a normal day's move: the ATR, the average daily range, is 10.47. A stop below 271.77 would be too easy to hit. No trade until a daily close holds inside 271.77–277.07, with 293.72 resistance as the first target.

decision.timing: With no earnings date in the data, forecast revisions and price levels set the timing. Options imply a move of about 3.9% by Nov 20, and the largest put open interest sits at the 280.0 and 275.0 strikes, right above the support zone.

change_mind: The next filing shows trailing free cash flow rising above 19.7B with operating margin holding at or above 33.32%. That would support buying closer to 282.31.
The 30-day change in this year's earnings estimate turns from -5.2% back above 0. That would mean forecasts have stopped falling, and I would buy at 280.2 rather than waiting for 277.07.
A daily close below 271.77 cancels the support-zone buy and moves the plan to 234.35. A daily close above 293.72 would reopen a swing entry.
payload.what_changed: Unchanged: the decision is still wait, because this year's earnings estimate fell another 5.2% in 30 days while free cash flow stays at 19.7B. Dipping just under 282.31 is not enough to buy, so the first buy level moves to 277.07 (it was 282.31 yesterday).
